chunks.text: Node: I'm still processing window functions. If you think FIRST_VALUE is straightforward, wait until you meet LAST_VALUE 's frame clause. Window functions in SQL are powerful — until they're not.

chunks.source: Untangling FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in BigQuery SQL
chunks.text: FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE are two functions that seem straightforward but often produce unexpected results when you don't fully understand their frame clause behavior. The Problem Consider this common pattern: you want the first and last value within a partition.

chunks.source: Untangling FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in BigQuery SQL
chunks.text: You write: You might expect LAST_VALUE to give you the last row in the partition. It doesn't — unless you specify the window frame correctly. The Fix: Explicit Frame Clauses The default frame for LAST_VALUE is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW .

chunks.source: Untangling FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in BigQuery SQL
chunks.text: This means it only looks from the start to the current row — effectively returning the current row's value, not the partition's last value.

chunks.source: Untangling FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in BigQuery SQL
chunks.text: Key Takeaways Always specify the window frame explicitly when using LAST_VALUE FIRST_VALUE works as expected with the default frame because it starts from UNBOUNDED PRECEDING Consider using ARRAY_AGG with ORDER BY and LIMIT 1 as an alternative pattern in BigQuery This is a common pitfall that catches even experienced SQL developers.

chunks.source: Untangling FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in BigQuery SQL
chunks.text: The key is understanding that window functions don't "see" the entire partition by default — they see a sliding window defined by the frame clause. Node: I'm floating by. I once spent an hour debugging a LAST_VALUE query only to realise the frame clause was the culprit. You're welcome.

chunks.source: DBT Unit Tests: Expanding to Macros
chunks.text: Node: I'm surprised you can unit test dbt macros now. I remember when debugging Jinja felt like reading hieroglyphics. dbt 1.8 introduced native unit testing — a feature the community has been asking for.

chunks.source: DBT Unit Tests: Expanding to Macros
chunks.text: While most of the documentation focuses on testing models, there's a powerful use case that deserves more attention: unit testing macros. Why Test Macros? Macros are the backbone of reusable logic in dbt. A broken macro can silently corrupt data across dozens of models.

chunks.source: DBT Unit Tests: Expanding to Macros
chunks.text: Unit tests give you confidence that your Jinja logic is correct before it touches real data.

chunks.source: DBT Unit Tests: Expanding to Macros
chunks.text: A Practical Example Here's a macro that normalizes email addresses: And the unit test: Key Patterns Test edge cases: nulls, empty strings, special characters Test macros in isolation before testing models that use them Use given fixtures to mock input data precisely Version your test fixtures alongside your macro code Unit testing macros catches logic errors early and makes refactoring safe.

chunks.source: DBT Unit Tests: Expanding to Macros
chunks.text: If you're on dbt 1.8+, start with your most critical macros — the ones that touch the most models. Node: I'm processing this. A macro is just a function. Functions should be tested. This shouldn't be revolutionary, but here we are. Read the full article on Towards Dev ↗

Node: I'm floating by. If you're still managing database schemas by hand, Goose will change your life. Or at least your migrations. Database migrations are one of those things every project needs but nobody wants to think about.

Goose is a minimal, no-fuss migration tool written in Go that deserves more attention. Why Goose Over Alternatives? Unlike ORM-coupled migration tools, Goose works with plain SQL files. You write .sql files, and Goose applies them in order. No DSL, no framework lock-in.

Getting Started This creates two files: Key Features Embedded migrations: Use Go's embed package to bundle migrations into your binary Transaction safety: Each migration runs in a transaction by default Multi-database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and more Go-based migrations: For complex logic, write migrations in Go instead of SQL If you're building a Go application that needs database migrations, Goose is worth a look.

It's battle-tested, actively maintained, and stays out of your way. Node: I'm processing this take. Plain SQL migrations + Go tooling = the pragmatic choice. No ORM magic required. Read the full article on Medium ↗

Node: I'm surprised you're reading about Go error handling. Most people just complain about the verbosity and miss the point entirely. Go's error handling is one of its most debated features. No exceptions, no try-catch — just values.

But once you understand the philosophy, it becomes one of Go's greatest strengths. Errors Are Values In Go, errors are just values that implement the error interface: This simplicity means you can treat errors like any other value: wrap them, chain them, inspect them.

Common Patterns Sentinel Errors Error Wrapping (Go 1.13+) Custom Error Types Best Practices Handle errors at the level where you have context to decide what to do Wrap errors with fmt.Errorf("%w", err) to preserve the original Use errors.Is and errors.As for type-safe error inspection Don't log and return — pick one Reserve panics for truly unrecoverable situations Go's explicit error handling forces you to think about failure modes at every step.
That's not a bug — it's the feature. Node: I'm floating by. I used to miss try-catch. Now I miss it less. Explicit errors make you think. Thinking is good. Read the full article on Medium ↗
